To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the air–water interfacial tension is a key factor determining how macromolecules adsorb to air–water interface, (2) the air–interfacial tension is reduced in the presence of surfactants, (3) surfactant adsorption to the air–liquid interface is a reversible equilibrium process, and (4) surfactants are not adsorbed to the liquid–liquid interfaces of water–water or water–buffer mixtures.
(i) macromolecules can become adsorbed to air–water surfaces, (ii) this adsorption is not necessarily a reversible process, and (iii) the process is not necessarily limited to the thinning process.

(i) protein monolayers can serve as sacrificial coverslips, (ii) the protein monolayers are stable for at least several hours, and (iii) the monolayers do not significantly alter the appearance of protein crystals.

the development of structure-friendly sample preparation methods.
the question of how to best prepare samples for single-particle cryo-EM.
the question of how macromolecules interact with air–water interfaces and how to avoid such interactions in the course of sample preparation for single-particle cryo-EM.

there is no single solution to the problem, but rather a number of possible solutions.
the risk of interfacial interactions is real, that it is difficult to assess, that it can be reduced, and that it should be taken seriously.
there is a need for further research in the direction of structure-friendly sample preparation methods.

the preparation of samples for single-particle cryo-EM is still an area of active development, with many possible improvements yet to be made.
the risk of interfacial denaturation is not as large as it may seem at first sight, but it is also not as negligible as we would have hoped.
the air–water surface is a hazardous place for macromolecules, and we must take steps to avoid it.

the air–water interfacial interactions of protein molecules are very sensitive to their environment.
the risk of interfacial adsorption of proteins and nucleic acids is very real.
it is important to be aware of the hazards that macromolecules face when they are confined to thin films of water.
